sections.title: Core Foundations & Conceptual Framework
sections.content:
• **Hydrological Cycle & Water Budget**: India receives an estimated annual precipitation of about 4,000 billion cubic meters (BCM), out of which only about 1,869 BCM is the **average annual water availability**, and usable water is restricted to approximately 1,123 BCM.
• **Surface vs. Groundwater Split**: Total surface water flow is estimated at 690 BCM, while total replenishable groundwater potential is around **446 BCM**, highlighting the dual reliance of the agrarian economy on both sectors.
• **Basin Approach**: India is divided into **20 river basins** (major basins having catchment areas > 20,000 sq. km) which form the primary hydrological planning units for inland water management.
• **Key Metric / Factor**: Per capita water availability is declining steadily due to population growth, pushing India closer to the **water stress threshold** of 1,700 cubic meters per person per year and absolute water scarcity below 1,000 cubic meters.

items.definition: The quantity of groundwater that gets recharged annually from rainfall, canal seepage, return flow from irrigation, and water bodies, forming the basis of annual withdrawal limits.
Nutrient enrichment of water bodies (via agricultural runoff and sewage) leading to algal blooms, depletion of dissolved oxygen, and eventual choking of aquatic ecosystems.
Statutory body established under the IWAI Act (1985) for development and regulation of national waterways for shipping and navigation.

items.term: Central Water Commission (CWC) & Central Ground Water Board (CGWB)
items.definition: Apex technical bodies under the Ministry of Jal Shakti responsible for hydrological data collection, flood forecasting, basin planning, and groundwater assessment.

items.title: Major Geographical Distribution / Regional Hubs
items.content:
• **Gangetic-Brahmaputra Basin**: Accounts for nearly 60% of India's total surface water resources, supported by massive alluvial aquifers and dense canal networks.
• **Peninsular River Basins**: Godavari, Krishna, and Cauvery basins feature extensive multipurpose dam infrastructure, tank irrigation (Southern plateau), and intense inter-state water disputes.

items.title: Challenges, Reforms & Forward Strategy
items.content:
• **Bottlenecks / Issues**: Over-extraction of groundwater in Northwest India (Punjab, Haryana), geogenic contamination (arsenic in Ganga-Brahmaputra plains, fluoride in hard-rock terrain), and untreated industrial effluents.
• **Policy Interventions**: Jal Jeevan Mission (Har Ghar Jal), Atal Bhujal Yojana for sustainable groundwater management, National Hydrology Project, and Namami Gange.

items.title: Mnemonic for Major Peninsular Rivers (North to South)
items.content:
• **Memory Acronym / Phrase**: "**M**ahanadi **G**oes **K**avery, **P**eriyar **T**urns"
• **Decoded Meaning**: Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna, Pennar, Cauvery, Periyar, Vaigai (Order of major east-flowing and southern peninsular rivers).
• **Prelims Exam Value**: Instantly solves map-based chronological sequencing questions from North to South.

items.title: Retention Rule of Thumb
items.content: • **Core Formula / Rule**: Remember that Peninsular rivers are **older, wider, and graded**, whereas Himalayan rivers are **younger, deep-cutting (gorges), and aggrading** in the plains.

upscNotes.content: Examiner Trap: UPSC frequently confuses natural freshwater lakes with coastal brackish lagoons or crater lakes. For instance, Chilika is a brackish water coastal lagoon (not a freshwater inland lake), while Lonar is a meteor-impact crater lake in basaltic terrain.

Mains Value Addition: Emphasize the transition from 'Supply-side management' (building more dams) to 'Demand-side management' (micro-irrigation, crop diversification, aquifer mapping under aquifer management plans) for sustainable water security.

keyTakeaways: Inland water resources comprise both surface and groundwater, heavily skewed regionally towards the Gangetic-Brahmaputra plains.
Institutional mechanisms like CWC, CGWB, and IWAI govern resource assessment, conservation, and navigation.
Severe challenges of over-extraction, contamination, and climate variability necessitate a shift to decentralized demand-side watershed management.
